title: A Harmless Act of Halloween Rebellion
summary: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic’s archives to contextualize the present. Sign up here.Last Halloween, I answered a knock on the door to find a young trick-or-treater dressed as a toilet. Not just any toilet—Skibidi Toilet, a disembodied head that pops out ...
content:
This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic’s archives to contextualize the present. Sign up here.

Last Halloween, I answered a knock on the door to find a young trick-or-treater dressed as a toilet. Not just any toilet—Skibidi Toilet, a disembodied head that pops out of a toilet and is a villain of the eponymous YouTube miniseries about an army of such creatures conquering Earth. I was visibly puzzled and asked him a series of questions. Was Skibidi his first name and Toilet his surname? Was he a man stuck in a toilet, or a new, hybrid organism? He looked at his friends and laughed; I smiled awkwardly as I distributed Airheads.

When I was a kid, Halloween featured a reliably recognizable cast: Darth Vaders, Little Mermaids, and plenty of Spidermen. But the internet’s memes have inevitably bled into costumes. For every zombie, there is now also a John Pork (an anthropomorphic pig in a red flannel that keeps calling your phone), a Ballerina Cappuccina (a cappuccino that performs ballet in a pink tutu), and a Tung Tung Tung Sahur. (Sahur is an AI-generated bipedal kentongan drum with a human face that wields a baseball bat. He’s also Italian.)

Wearing a costume that successfully confounds grown-ups could be considered a harmless act of Halloween rebellion on a day known for mischief. This holiday has long marked an occasion for kids to assert an us-versus-them mentality toward adults. In 2012, Emily Chertoff compiled a history of the Halloween pranks for The Atlantic, recounting how the antics once got so out of control that in 1923, Omaha’s “police commissioner came up with a solution: he would recruit 500 of the city’s ‘worst boys’ to serve as ‘special policemen’ on Halloween, turning over to each a badge and a beat.” Soon enough, “every boy in the city” wanted to qualify, according to an anonymous author in The New York Times.

For decades, cities introduced creative solutions to quell the discord on All Hallows’ Eve. In 1938, “Boston’s police commissioner gave ‘engraved awards’ to ‘the three schools in districts which showed the “least vandalism” on Halloween,’” Chertoff noted. She explained that after World War II, trick-or-treating took off as one of the most successful interventions to actually stem Halloween’s mayhem. It also led many people to lament the death of the holiday. “The children who come to my door will remember All Hallows’ Eve as a night when they sold their right to rebellion for some sugar in expensive wrappings,” Lois Phillips Hudson wrote in this magazine in 1962.

The rebellious spirit of Halloween wasn’t gone, though. Costumes were another battleground between kids and grown-ups, and the freedom to express oneself was at the center of this clash. “On Halloween a boy can’t wear anything feminine. The idea of lipstick horrifies a father,” Evelyn Goodenough Pitcher quoted one mother saying in The Atlantic’s March 1963 issue. The generational divide has taken on a new form in today’s algorithm-inflected celebration. In 2024, Kate Lindsay argued against such niche costumes. “The meme invasion threatens the spirit of Halloween,” she wrote in The Atlantic. “The costumes aren’t intended for my—or any other partygoer’s—consumption. They’re for our phones.”

Indeed, at a Halloween party I attended in Bushwick, I bumped into someone dressed as the grandfather who ate paint thinking it was yogurt (a real person whose image became a meme). Last year, photos went viral of adults donning “six-seven” outfits at Halloween, sounding the death knell for the meme. Children, though, aren’t always performing for the algorithm. Maybe their real Halloween joy comes from laughing at a perplexed adult holding a candy bowl on their porch.

Although pranks have faded from Halloween’s traditions—the “trick” has surrendered to the “treat”—little rebellions remain. The mischief-makers of the early 20th century might have been pleased to see legions of giggling Tung Tung Tung Sahurs roaming the streets, while mystified parents ask one another: What’s your kid dressed as?

title: Democrats Are Ready to Run Hegseth ‘Out of Town’
summary: Many Democrats have a post-midterm dream that goes something like this: Pete Hegseth, the push-up-loving, beardo-mocking former Fox News host who has led the Pentagon for almost two years with bombast and theatrics, is either fired or hauled before their new majority in the House to face impeachment...
content:
Many Democrats have a post-midterm dream that goes something like this: Pete Hegseth, the push-up-loving, beardo-mocking former Fox News host who has led the Pentagon for almost two years with bombast and theatrics, is either fired or hauled before their new majority in the House to face impeachment—which would make him just the third Cabinet secretary in history to face such a sanction. “One of the first things we’re going to do in the majority, we’re going to run Pete Hegseth out of town,” Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to be speaker of the House should the Democrats win that chamber, declared at a rally this month, the closest he’s come to saying the I-word.

Many of his colleagues feel the same. Hegseth helped steer the U.S. into war with Iran, and then failed to deliver victory. He initiated strikes against speedboats allegedly carrying narco-traffickers off the coasts of South and Central America that many Democrats view as extrajudicial killings. He pushed out scores of seasoned generals, many of whom were held in high esteem on Capitol Hill. All the while, he has flouted any notion of congressional oversight. His acidly partisan approach to Hill relations dates back to his contentious 2025 confirmation process, when he broke tradition by declining courtesy calls with most Democratic senators. And he has, in his political opponents’ view, brought a macho crassness to the job, railing against “fatties,” “weirdos,” and “beardos” and introducing hormone supplements to ensure “high T” troops. Former President Obama last weekend mocked the well-coiffed Hegseth for focusing on “the jawlines and testosterone levels of our troops” and for being consumed by vanity. “How much time,” Obama asked, “do you think this defense secretary spends looking at himself in the mirror in the morning?”

From a Democratic standpoint, what’s not to impeach? Yet precisely because Hegseth and his behavior present such a ripe target for House Democrats, they might ultimately decide against pursuing that measure. After all, even if a Democratic-controlled House voted to impeach Hegseth, and even if the Democrats win a majority in the Senate and convene a trial, Hegseth almost certainly would retain enough support in the upper chamber to fall short of the required 67 votes for conviction. The alternative is for Democrats to try to rein in Hegseth without the spectacle of impeachment, relying instead on the aggressive pursuit of their more traditional oversight mechanisms—hearings, investigations, and conditions attached to the annual defense budget. If Democrats are going to go to war, as it were, with the self-styled secretary of war, they may prefer to fight a battle they think they can actually win.

If Thomas Massie has his way, Hegseth’s impeachment wouldn’t wait until the new Congress convenes in January. The outgoing Republican representative from Kentucky has said he plans to bring the articles of impeachment he filed this fall against Hegseth up for a vote during the House’s lame-duck postelection session. His eight draft articles include accusations that Hegseth plotted to conduct an illegal war in Iran (a conflict for which President Trump never sought congressional authorization) and that he approved the “kidnapping of a sovereign foreign leader,” a reference to the January seizure of the Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro. Massie told Puck he thinks other Republicans who are poised to leave Congress may rally behind him. The vote to proceed with impeachment and the impeachment itself require a simple majority in the House.

[Read: Here’s who Democrats want to impeach next]

Democrats would likely welcome Massie’s move, even if it did no more than force Speaker Mike Johnson and Trump to come to Hegseth’s defense. A recent Politico poll showed that 63 percent of Democratic midterm voters would support impeaching the defense secretary. (Only Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was a more popular target for impeachment, with 65 percent support.) And, should Massie’s effort fail, the Democrats have their own draft articles at hand. Representative Yassamin Ansari of Arizona filed impeachment articles against Hegseth in April. Her draft articles are similar to Massie’s but also include accusations of obstructing congressional oversight and mishandling classified information (in March 2025, Hegseth shared sensitive war plans in a Signal group that included The Atlantic’s editor in chief). Her effort has 16 co-sponsors, all of them Democrats, but she sees the ground shifting and holds out hope that Trump will get rid of his defense secretary before Congress has the chance to act. “The calls against Hegseth’s leadership have increased dramatically on both sides of the aisle,” Ansari told us. “We are really strongly pushing the president to replace Hegseth.”

The White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told us in a statement that Trump strongly supports Hegseth. “Secretary Hegseth is doing a great job leading the Pentagon,” she said. Pentagon Press Secretary Kingsley Wilson called Hegseth a “transformative leader” who has “slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way.”

The House has impeached only two Cabinet secretaries: William Belknap, the secretary of war, in 1876; and Alejandro Mayorkas, the secretary of homeland security, in 2024. (In both cases, the Senate did not convict.)

Representative Jason Crow of Colorado, a Democrat and former Army Ranger, was one of the seven impeachment managers during Trump’s first impeachment trial in the Senate, in 2020. He told us the party needed to be cautious in considering a third presidential impeachment. But he is far less squeamish about trying to remove Hegseth. “Pete Hegseth and the corruption he’s brought to the Department of Defense is at the top of my list,” Crow said.

[Read: The Top Gun: Maverick theory of Pete Hegseth]

Representative Adam Smith, who would lead the House Armed Services Committee should Democrats take over, told us that he and his colleagues will have limited powers even in the majority, especially if the administration rebuffs congressional requests for documents or witnesses. The Justice Department, for instance, under Trump’s onetime personal attorney Todd Blanche, may decline to enforce congressional subpoenas. That would make even lawmakers like Smith, typically more inclined to dig into the arcana of acquisition reform than stage a made-for-TV trial, more likely to consider the toughest sanction.

“Do we try to work in a reasonable place or do we go right for the jugular here?” Smith said, referring to Jeffries’s desire to see Hegseth removed from office. “Personally I think there’s no reason to expect that Trump and Hegseth are going to cooperate with us in any way. So I think that Hakeem may well be right.” The decision could amount to an early test of Jeffries and his ability to corral the different factions in the Democratic caucus. Even as he has talked lately about running Hegseth out of town, Jeffries hasn’t explicitly endorsed an impeachment strategy. “Pete Hegseth needs to be pushed aside by the president,” he told MS NOW this week, “or we’re going to have to deal with the situation if he is not.”

GOP grumbling about Hegseth’s performance has intensified over the past year. Representative Mike Rogers and Senator Roger Wicker, the chairs of the House and Senate Armed Services Committees, respectively, have objected to administration plans to cut the U.S. military presence in Europe and to Pentagon delays in providing aid to Ukraine. Senator Susan Collins and others complained when Hegseth fired respected military leaders, including Generals Randy George and Chris “C. D.” Donahue. Mike Johnson panned Hegseth’s plan to livestream an execution by firing squad. (Trump ultimately quashed the livestream.) Outgoing Senator Thom Tillis has described his vote to confirm Hegseth as the “biggest regret” of his career. Still, even those Republicans unimpressed with Hegseth have been loath to cross the president, and they continue to support most of Hegseth’s plans, including a boost in defense spending to $1.5 trillion.

[Read: How Pete Hegseth’s plan for a reality-TV execution imploded]

That suggests an uphill push for a conviction in the Senate—and a trial would provide Hegseth with a prominent, televised perch from which he could lambast the effort, secure in the knowledge that his prospects of conviction are remote. That may be all the more desirable for him as Trump enters his lame-duck years and the MAGA faithful search for a worthy successor. The spectacle of Hegseth in a congressional hearing room defending his troops and hitting back against Democrats could boost the presidential ambitions he is said to harbor. Trump’s two impeachments ultimately helped his political standing by giving him a clear foe; Republicans might welcome a similar dynamic with the secretary of defense in the dock.

Should Democrats decide against impeachment proceedings, they are likely instead to resort to more common oversight measures. Riders to the defense-spending legislation could compel the Pentagon to comply with congressional mandates barring troop drawdowns around the world. Admiral Mitch Bradley, the head of U.S. Special Operations Command, will likely face questions over a September 2, 2025, air strike that killed two men clinging to maritime wreckage in the Caribbean. Democratic lawmakers also want to declassify the Office of Legal Counsel memo that lays out a legal rationale for those operations, and potentially bring in military lawyers to testify. Admiral Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. military operations in the Middle East, could be asked about casualties from the Iran war—those of American troops and Iranian civilians—and damage to U.S. bases in the region. But all of these efforts would be politically fraught for Democrats, whom Republicans are sure to accuse of going after the troops.

Lawmakers told us they still don’t know the true state of the Navy’s Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain and other facilities that have been attacked, other than that they have sustained real damage. When Democratic Senator Chris Murphy made a fact-finding trip to Qatar this month, the Pentagon denied him permission to visit Al Udeid, the military’s regional air hub, which was struck by Iran, and barred military officials from briefing him. Lawmakers will push Hegesth on whether the military was negligent in protecting U.S. forces from Iranian drones and missiles—21 service members have died and more than 800 have been wounded in the conflict—and subjecting sailors to a record-breaking stint at sea. “My north star is anything jeopardizing the immediate safety and well-being of our troops,” Crow told us. “Are they getting equipment they need? Why is he firing the top ranks of the Army? There are a lot of questions.” The Pentagon may also be pressed to provide details of business deals made as part of Hegseth’s race to move the military into the age of artificial intelligence or to purchase Venezuelan oil.

All of that presumes, of course, that Hegseth remains in office. Trump has shown no inclination to fire him, though the White House may look for scapegoats in the event of a midterm drubbing. The Cabinet official most closely associated with the Iran war could fit the bill. Or Trump could find an off-ramp for Hegseth. Rumors abound at the Pentagon that the president will prevail on Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee to name Hegseth to her vacant seat should she win her race for Tennessee governor, as she’s expected to do. A spokeswoman for Blackburn’s campaign said the senator would not have any discussions about a potential replacement “until the appropriate time”; the Pentagon’s Wilson said the Blackburn idea was “nothing more than Beltway gossip by anonymous sources.” The White House declined to comment on the idea. Were it to happen, Democrats might be satisfied that Hegseth is out of the Pentagon—but less pleased to have him as a colleague.

title: The Rise of the Sexy-Cozy Autumn Read
summary: Unto every season is given a certain kind of book. When the new year beckons a new you, self-help thrives. Breezy beach reads rule the summer. Cookbook recommendations abound in the lead-up to Thanksgiving. Curiously, publishers told me, Easter is big for picture books (which are easy to stick in a ...
content:
Unto every season is given a certain kind of book. When the new year beckons a new you, self-help thrives. Breezy beach reads rule the summer. Cookbook recommendations abound in the lead-up to Thanksgiving. Curiously, publishers told me, Easter is big for picture books (which are easy to stick in a basket next to the chocolate bunny). And Halloween is for horror. Time to bust out some Shirley Jackson (or perhaps some Stephen King or Edgar Allan Poe).

Yet the days of decorative gourds and darkening evenings have also become a boom season for romance novels—not just any romance novels, but ones targeted at both Halloween and fall more broadly. These books exist on a spectrum of snuggly to spooky: on one end, crispy foliage and adorable bookshops; on the other, the growing subgenre of horror romance. In the middle lie Halloweeny but still-sweet stories of witches brewing love potions, grim reapers falling for guardian angels, and regular old humans getting entangled with creatures of all kinds. This trend results from a brew of ingredients that include market forces, social-media trends, and readers yearning to escape the real world for a cozier one with more regular seasons.

Autumnal romances are not an entirely new phenomenon, but they have really taken off in the past two to five years. Winter-holiday-themed romances used to be published around the end of September, according to Leah Hultenschmidt, the publisher of Hachette Book Group’s romance-focused Forever imprint. “People talk about the Christmas creep. But we were really creeping it,” she told me. Now, she said, holiday books are being pushed back because “fall has become its own selling season.”

[Read: The publishing industry’s most swoon-worthy genre]

Taylor Capizola, the general manager of the romance bookstore The Ripped Bodice in Los Angeles, told me that The Ex Hex by Erin Stirling was the first “overtly autumnal, overtly Halloweeny” book she noticed catching on. That book—about a witch who curses her ex-boyfriend—came out in 2021. That same year, Jeannie Chin released the small-town romance novel The Inn on Sweetbriar Lane. It’s set in fall, and features a pumpkin festival. But Chin told me that at the time, she wasn’t thinking of it as a seasonal romance, and her publisher wasn’t really planning to market it that way. (The cover, with its pink flowers, actually looks pretty spring-y.) “As it came out, I think, is sort of when this ‘fall is the new Christmas’ thing started,” she said. “So we sort of pivoted with the marketing a little bit to take advantage of the fact that it absolutely is a fall book.”

Interest has escalated since then. Whereas in the early part of this decade, Capizola might have seen five or so Halloweeny books come into the shop in the fall, by last year The Ripped Bodice was unpacking “boxes and boxes and boxes,” she said. “Just a massive amount.” One of the fall-themed novels that came out this year was Chin’s. With The Cozy Nook Bookshop, “the idea of putting that fall cozy piece front and center was there from the beginning,” Chin said. This time, it has pumpkins on the cover.

To be fair to fall, it is very romantic. The leaves, the chill, the steamy beverages, and the beckoning of the fireplace all set the mood for what many hopeful singles call “cuffing season.” The beloved rom-com You’ve Got Mail famously takes place in fall, with Tom Hanks rhapsodizing about “a bouquet of newly sharpened pencils”—a quote that makes the rounds on social media every autumn.

But there’s romance set in the fall, and then there’s fall romance. “We are giving them something seasonal on purpose,” Hultenschmidt said of her publishing imprint. And seasonal romances can be very on the nose. Take Emily Henry’s 2020 romance, a beach read titled Beach Read, that is set at a lakeside beach town and stars an author who writes beach reads. Cindy Hwang, the editorial director at Berkley, which publishes Henry, told me she thinks that the popularity of Beach Read helped launch the trend of highly literal seasonal romances. Some of these fall books practically grab you by the collar, shove a pointy hat on your head, and pour a pumpkin-spice latte down your throat. For instance, last September, Amazon published a collection of short stories for Kindle and audiobook called Scared Sexy, one of which is about a sexy sleep-paralysis demon. All of the stories feature creatures, and most mention Halloween in some way. A couple of these stories were among Kindle’s most-purchased romance books of 2025, according to the blog Romancing the Data, which tracks romance best sellers.

For the same reason someone might watch scary movies or carve a pumpkin, they pick up sexy Halloween books to get into the spirit of the season. But why is seasonality something readers are particularly craving now? It may partly follow from the rise of “spooky season” as a concept. The phrase doesn’t seem to have been used much before 2018 or so, according to Google Trends. It’s invoked as a way of extending the playfully scary energy of Halloween throughout the fall, and giving adults an excuse to partake in seasonal delights along with kids.

Hultenschmidt suggested that the whole snuggly-to-spooky spectrum could be explained by the sense of uncertainty and instability pervading the culture right now. In the face of economic anxiety and political tension, people may seek safety in the comfort of a romance novel and its guaranteed happily-ever-after. Or “they want the terror of a horror novel to be like ‘Oh, well thank God it’s not this bad,’” she said. This might also explain the appeal of hybrid horror-romance books like this year’s Kiss Slay Replay by Rachel Harrison, about a woman trapped in a time loop at her best friend’s wedding, with a masked killer on the rampage and a handsome wedding guest to help her fight back.

[Read: The dark reality behind ‘cozy mysteries’]

I also wonder if some of the appeal is a result of climate change. Seasons other than summer are getting shorter, and all seasons are becoming more unpredictable. When I spoke with Hwang earlier this month, the high in our respective East Coast cities (D.C. and New York) was nearly 80 degrees. If I wanted to catch that classic fall feeling in mid-October this year, I would’ve been better served by cracking open a book than by going outside.

In addition to the comfort and the spookiness, all of the attention on fall stems from one more thing: marketing. Romance and autumn may go together these days like apple cider and cinnamon sticks, but that’s in part because each is having a moment that businesses have seized on.

Retailers have greatly expanded their lines of fall-coded decor, food, candles, and more. Cozy as a marketing aesthetic caught on during the pandemic and never quite left. Seasonal swag is a built-in yearly sales opportunity, no less so in publishing than in any other business.

At the same time, romance has become so successful that it could be said to be propping up the entire publishing industry. The genre is also a particularly fast-paced business. Many romance readers read a lot—Capizola told me some of her customers can read two novels in a day—and romance writers oblige their fans’ appetites with a regular supply of new books. Take Christina Lauren, the pen name of two best friends who co-write their books. Some years they have released two or even three full-length novels. This pace may make it easier to jump on trends relatively quickly, compared with genres where longer lead times are the standard. “Romance as a genre is currently driven in many ways by online trends,” Jamie Fortin, the founder of Friends to Lovers bookstore in Alexandria, Virginia, told me. (The exploding category of romantasy—romance plus fantasy—owes a lot to social-media hype, as well.)

[Read: The fan-fiction friendship that fueled a romance-novel empire]

It certainly helps that a seasonal read lends itself well to social media. TikTok and Instagram often favor books that evoke a recognizable aesthetic. On book covers, “you see the palettes are orange and yellow and purple,” Hultenschmidt said, in part so that everything looks “harmonious and beautiful” in recommendation-roundup posts. Some of these books seem to be aimed directly at the “cozy, witchy reads for fall” videos that pop up on BookTok. And when they hit their mark, they really hit it.

The Pumpkin Spice Café by Laurie Gilmore won the TikTok Shop Book of the Year award in 2024, seemingly on the sheer strength of its autumn aura. (Having read it, I don’t think it could have been on the strength of the prose, plot, or characters.) On StoryGraph and Goodreads, many readers proclaim they read it “for the vibes.” And it does check just about every trope box: pumpkin-spice lattes, a small-town “fall festival” complete with a Halloween costume contest, a possible haunting, a sexy, flannel-wearing farmer.

The danger of the fall-book boom (insofar as comfort reads can possibly be dangerous) is that chasing trends can lead to shallower art. Capizola put it diplomatically: “It becomes something more like a collectible than it is actually just about the content within the book itself.” But the best seasonal romances are more than a jumble of poorly executed tropes in a trench coat—they manage to fuse vibes with craft and heart.

A good example is Sangu Mandanna’s The Very Secret Society of Irregular Witches, which was originally published in the lead-up to spooky season 2022. It’s the story of a witch who is lonely by occupation—witches aren’t supposed to gather for fear of attracting unwanted attention. Nonetheless, she takes a job as a tutor to three charming, rambunctious young witches who are illicitly living together at an enchanted estate in the English countryside. She bands together with the quirky caretakers of the home—including a grumpy, hot librarian—to protect the children from impending disaster. It’s totally charming.

This book seems to be living the dream of any seasonal romance—I’ve noticed it bubbling back up on social media and StoryGraph’s most popular list every fall since it was published. When something is pegged to fall, it has a short retail window, “but you have the opportunity to promote year after year,” Hultenschmidt said. But to become a perennial, a title needs to be pretty special, or at least lucky enough to capture attention quickly, because these books’ time in the waning fall sunlight is limited. By just a couple of weeks ago, when I was doing interviews for this story, Christmas romances were already hitting the shelves.

title: The Variety Bag Has Ruined Halloween
summary: All Halloween candy is the same now. Nothing stands out, apart from the quantity of candy dumped out on the floor back home. Every house seems to buy a variety bag of seemingly random candy, and consequently every stop metes out a little more of the same treats as the previous one did or the next on...
content:
All Halloween candy is the same now. Nothing stands out, apart from the quantity of candy dumped out on the floor back home. Every house seems to buy a variety bag of seemingly random candy, and consequently every stop metes out a little more of the same treats as the previous one did or the next one will. A harvesttime holiday that evolved from traditional reflections on death is now merely another household chore to carry out on the way to mortal life’s certain end.

In my memory, the trick-or-treating procedure used to go down like this: An older lady or stern man made some idle chatter about costumes and then dispensed one or three candies into my bag directly from their basket. The candy provided was particular and intentional: You got a Hershey’s Special Dark mini and a wee Mr. Goodbar, perhaps, or a few Smarties cylinders, or, alas, a handful of Bit-O-Honeys. Children identified houses by what they dispensed: Don’t miss the quiet bungalow that yielded a surprising payload of Rolos, but don’t bother with the big, well-manicured property on the corner where only Brach’s Jelly Nougats are on offer. Such impressions sometimes became sufficiently evocative—the Rolo house—to characterize a street’s residences at other times of the year.

Not anymore. Kids’ hauls at each house are bigger than ever, but also more similar. Back when the seasonal candy was more diverse, it communicated something about the trick-or-treatee’s aesthetics and even their values. Hershey’s bars or Tootsie Roll Pops suggested traditionalism. So did shortened tubes of Necco wafers (in an esoteric way), or cellophane-wrapped, spherical hard candies (in an antiquated one). Baby Ruth or Butterfinger insinuated indulgence, moderated—Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups meant it immoderately. A miniature box of Nerds or a Blow Pop would have come across as progressive, at least during my youth. A packet of Pop Rocks would have felt positively punk rock.

[Read: A Halloween myth that can finally die]

Kids might share intelligence about the house offering Boston Baked Beans (actually good, but considered undesirable by peers) or Red Hots (symbolically righteous but actually underwhelming). A handful of Sixlets—previously unheard-of—implied a larger universe than a pre-internet child might have imagined possible. Some houses matched a kid’s unexplained taste in quiet, affirming ways. For me, Spree was a peculiar pleasure, and Chuckles jelly candies, and 3 Musketeers bars, with their gentle, whipped nougat. Some doors suggested eccentricity or extremism. Even after the razor-blade panic and Tylenol scare, some homes still gave out plastic-wrapped, homemade popcorn balls, an earnest but unwelcome attempt to retain the disappearing past. Others came off as unhinged. Dentists sometimes offered pencils or crayons instead of candy, for obvious reasons. My parents insisted on throwing handfuls of nickels into awaiting pillowcases, a practice that caused me enormous shame despite the fact that some neighborhood children appreciated it.

This opportunity to express distinctiveness at the Halloween stoop, and to receive it, has become much harder. In part, that’s because trick-or-treating has declined in general. The reasons are many: The total number of trick-or-treat-age children has decreased by a quarter since 1970; community trunk-or-treats or school events in the days leading up to Halloween started supplanting the door-to-door tradition; parents and kids decamp for “better” neighborhoods, whose betterness begets ever-increasing Hallows’ Eve inequity. Neighborhoods are less connected in general, and some municipalities enforce nanny-state ordinances around the practice.

But the candy has also changed. Like soda or fast food, candy was largely regional until well beyond the middle of the century. The Oh Henry! Bar, for example, was invented around 1920, by one account named after an exclamation a clerk at George Williamson’s Chicago candy store uttered to a frequent patron named Henry. But consolidation came to the candy industry. Hershey bought Reese’s in 1963, then Almond Joy and others. Mars ended up with M&M’s, Snickers, Twix, Milky Way, and many more. These days, those two companies account for around two thirds of the U.S. chocolate market. Along the way, products such as Oh Henry! fell by the wayside. That bar changed hands four times from 1965 to 2019, when it was taken off the market in the United States. Now no American child needs to ask a parent what the heck an Oh Henry! bar is, because they definitely won’t receive one in their plastic jack-o’-lantern.

October retail flyers of the past reveal much greater choices. In 1970 and 1985, Kmart advertised bags of Milk Duds, Whoppers, Dots, Sugar Daddy, Good & Plenty, and Junior Mints, among others. A 1988 coupon ad from the Leaf candy company (once the fourth-largest North American confectioner, most of whose brands were bought by Hershey in 1996) sold packs of Chuckles (my heart!), Slo Poke, Good & Fruity, Zagnut, and Rain-Blo bubble gum. Even products from companies that have survived brand acquisitions used to be more varied: Hershey’s Kisses were a common trick-or-treat offering, for example, and Tootsie Roll Industries sold bags of Tootsie Roll Pops. Now, at my local supermarket, Haribo Goldbears represent the sole independent exception.

More often today, Halloween candy comes in those nefarious variety bags. This practice isn’t entirely new; a variety of Hershey’s minis—Milk Chocolate, Special Dark, Krackel, and Mr. Goodbar—were a tradition of office reception desks as much as dark neighborhoods on October 31. Now assortments are the norm. This year, I found several nearly identical Hershey’s bundles at my local Dierbergs, each containing its namesake chocolate bars along with Reese’s cups, KitKat, Almond Joy—and then an oddball from the farm leagues, such as Milk Duds, Hershey’s Cookies ‘n’ Creme, or Rolo. Reese’s Pieces, a candy that E.T. once made unique, were available only in a package with KitKat, Reese’s cups, and two types of Jolly Rancher gummies. Mars has its own versions with Snickers, Milky Way, and two kinds of M&Ms.

The industrial consolidation has turned Halloween candy into an anonymous murk. That mix probably pleases every trick-or-treater a little, but it also risks making every house’s offering essentially identical.

Across the street at Costco, the situation was even more dire. Enormous bags of Kirkland Signature Favorites were on offer, each containing a fusion of the other fusions: Mars and Hershey and Haribo candies all mixed together. The collection was so haphazard and homogeneous, Costco felt obliged to emblazon a large disclaimer on the packaging’s front: “This bag may not include all varieties listed.” A handful of candy an adult might dispense from the Costco superset is identical to one taken from a child’s overall plunder.

The point is clear: Nobody should care what kind of treats they buy or receive anymore. All Halloween candy is what economists call a perfect substitute for other candy. Throw a bag in the cart and get the candy-having done with—then hold out the basket of whatever came in the bag and let the kiddos get the candy-taking done with too.

Perhaps the indifference counts as apathy rather than disdain. Candy might just not be as important as it used to be. Changing tastes have led to an ever-widening set of options for, and conceptions of, treats: sweet beverages, frozen desserts, snack products, yogurt-alikes, breakfast cereals and bars, cookies and cakes. Sweet coffeehouse beverages, limited-edition cookies and snacks, and endless brand collaborations have also created more options and greater surface area for candy alternatives. Competition, combined with a long moral and dental disapproval of sweets, has contracted candy’s charm.

[Read: The costume I can’t persuade my husband to throw away]

Almost a decade ago, in one of the most unpopular opinions I have ever published, I wrote that full-size candy bars have no place on Halloween. My argument was that big candy bars counted as normal ones, and that Halloween (understood as a holiday of sweets rather than death) was best experienced by amassing and experiencing the treats in a novel and different form. But even all those years ago, I failed to understand how far candy bars had fallen. Full-size ones had already become unfamiliar, such that discovering them on Halloween counted as the novelty that fun-size diversity had represented. Once, a neighborhood’s children could steer one another toward the house with the Reese’s Pieces, or away from the one with the Mounds (sorry, Mounds). But now the only possible take on candy is that yours is better because it is bigger, and you are therefore better because you are more affluent: That house has full-size bars!

So this year, amid the bulging plastic duffels of candy at the Costco, I found myself reconsidering the wickedness of big bars. My wife and I searched our memories of youth, ever more distant, for precedents. Big bars were rarer then, but not unheard-of. When available, we recalled, they did not typically suggest wealth but modesty matched to tribute: mostly big, plain Hershey’s bars, offered by older couples for whom the candy bore particular meaning, because Hershey had transformed chocolate from an unattainable luxury into a cheap, accessible staple.

Then, just beside the anonymous mixed bag, boxes of full-size bars stacked on pallets met my eye. Costco was selling 30 to a box, with Hershey’s, Hershey’s With Almond, the Reese’s Peanut Butter Cup two pack, and the four-fingered KitKat. Even the full-size bars had been relegated to an assortment.

title: Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr

content:
Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website

Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.

Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.

title: Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official
summary: Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and possible treatmentThe “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials....
content:
Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and possible treatment

The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials.

As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies.

Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected to travel ban and asset freeze

Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.

A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.

Is it a deliberate military strategy?The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her ho...
content:
Exclusive: Coordinated airstrikes on territory held by al-Shabaab are driving the civilian population to find refuge alongside a river where rising water levels are a threat to safety. Is it a deliberate military strategy?

The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river.

“The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.”

content:
Rapid Support Forces strike five power stations in three states controlled by Sudanese army

Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have launched a coordinated drone attack against five power stations, causing mass power outages across the country’s east, a government official said.

The drones hit two power stations each in the states of Al-Jazira and Gedaref and one in White Nile state, “resulting in power outages across large parts of these three states”, the official said on condition of anonymity.
